commands.quote: I follow the brother inside to the warden

input: I follow the brother inside to the warden and hand over the sealed ledger.
reply:
Inside was stone-cool after the sun and smelled of tallow, vellum and crushed herbs. A long room ran the depth of the building, benches along one wall, an old brother grinding ink at a side table who looked up once and back down. Behind, the bell rang twice more, and soft footsteps moved toward the far end of the house.

Ansel led him down a short passage to a cell at the end, door already open. Warden Ambrose wrote at a sloped desk beneath the window—a spare grey man, sleeves inked to the second knuckle, a reading board propped against the inkwell. He glanced up at the two shadows in his doorway and set his pen across the well.

"Ansel."

"Alderwatch's courier, Warden."

At the threshold Alaric held out the ledger. Ansel received it in both hands, carried it across the room, and laid it on the desk, folding back the oiled cloth so the wax showed.

Ambrose lifted it to the window light without opening it. His thumb worked along the seal's edges, pressed the stamp, turned it over.

"Whole." He tapped the wax twice. "Unbroken wax. Half the packets that reach this house look like they lost an argument with the road." He cracked the seal with a small snap, riffled a page or two, and made a low sound of satisfaction at what he found there.

Then he looked up at Alaric properly, taking in the dust and the long walk.

"Well met, courier. Sit, if you'll sit—there's well water, and bread from this morning's oven yet." He nodded Ansel toward a shelf with a jug on it, half-rising from his own stool to make room on the bench by the desk. "How stood the road to you?"

input: I hand Bertho the parcel. "The fever draught is in the flask—two spoons at dawn and dusk—and the dried herbs make a tisane for the sweating. From Ansel at the physick hall."
reply:
Bertho took the parcel in both hands, turning it over once to check the waxed cloth, the string, the flask nestled firm against it. "Level all the way, then. Good." He worked a thumbnail under the knot, then seemed to think better of opening it in the yard and held it against his side instead.

"Two spoons at dawn and dusk, the flask. Tisane for the sweating." He repeated it back slowly, the way a man does when he means to keep it. "I'll write it on the doorframe with chalk if I have to. My head's not what it was."

He looked at the tollhouse door, and for a moment the tollkeeper's easy manner thinned. "She's sleeping, my girl. Senna, she's eight. Started burning yesterday night and by morning she couldn't keep water down." He cleared his throat and picked the axe up off the block, more for something to do with his hands than any need of kindling. "The hall said there'd be a runner today. I didn't rightly believe it would be today."

He stepped to the chain across the road and dropped its hook free, dragging it back against the tollhouse wall so the way stood open. "Foot travellers ride free anyhow, but there's the bridge, and there's standing in a doorway blocking it." A short laugh, mostly breath. "You've walked half a day. There's well water in there, and my wife baked yesterday—there's bread if you want a bite before you go back. No call to rush off hungry."

He held the tollhouse door open with his shoulder, the parcel still hugged against his ribs, waiting to see whether the runner would come in.

input: "Thank you, Hall master." I finish my tea and head back to the counter. "Maren — Greve said to leave word where I'm lodging with you. And I believe this day-book is yours to file." I hand it over. "Is there anywhere decent and cheap to sleep in Alderwatch?"
reply:
The door clicked shut behind him, and the hall took him back with its ordinary noise — boots on boards, a dog scratching itself by the hearth. Maren was at the counter with her ledger open, and she looked up as he came.

She took the day-book in both hands, checked something on the cover, and set it on the shelf behind her with the others.

"That's filed, then." She pulled a fresh slip toward her and dipped her pen. "Lodging. Where are you staying? I'll write it down plain, and if anything turns up from the rider or the yard, that's where you'll hear of it."

The pen waited over the paper.

"As for decent and cheap." She counted on her fingers. "The Wethered Ox, down past the grain market — clean straw, a lock on the door, eight copper a night, and the ale won't kill you. The Sleeping Bear near the east gate is a copper cheaper and a good deal less clean. And there's Widow Sarra's rooms on Cooper's Lane — she lets to Guild folk at six, and she feeds you porridge whether you want it or not. Me, I'd take the Ox if I wanted my own door, and Sarra's if I wanted hot food and someone who'd notice if I didn't come home." She said the last part flatly, without looking up from the slip, and scratched the pen's nib dry on the wood.

"Your pick. Tell me which, and I'll write it down."
